reflection.quote: The days are long, but the decades are short.
reflection.reading:
Late August Sundays have a particular weight to them. Summer is thinning out. There's a slight edge in the evening air that wasn't there two weeks ago. If you're newer to this, Sundays used to mean something else — a wreckage of a Saturday night, the promise to yourself that Monday would be different, the low static hum of shame under everything you tried to do with the day.

One of the quietest gifts of getting sober is what happens to Sunday. It stops being a day you're trying to survive and becomes a day you actually get to spend. Coffee that tastes like coffee. A book you can actually follow. A walk without needing to piece together what you said last night. The ordinariness of it is the point. Nothing dramatic is happening, and that's the miracle.

Altman's line cuts both ways. The days are long — this one, right now, stretched out in front of you, is genuinely long if you're present for it. And the decades are short — meaning the accumulation of these plain, sober Sundays is the whole life. Not the peaks. Not the trips or the milestones. The Sundays. Show up for this one the way it is. Read something. Call someone. Move your body. Make the small choices that the version of you a decade from now will look back on and thank you for.
reflection.meditation: What would it look like to spend today, not survive it?

affirmations: Today I get to have an ordinary Sunday, and that is not a small thing.
I am building a life out of the choices I make on quiet days like this one.
I am present for my own life, and I don't have to numb any part of it.

gratitude.prayer: Grateful for a Sunday morning that isn't spent piecing yesterday back together. Grateful for the boring, steady things — coffee, sunlight through the window, a phone that isn't buzzing with apologies I have to make. Grateful for the people who taught me that a quiet day is a good day, and for the version of me that kept showing up long enough to believe it.
gratitude.closing: One more ordinary day. One more day I get to keep.
